what_it_does: Portfolio optimization — picking the best mix of investments to maximize return for a given level of risk — boils down to solving a large system of linear equations. Quantum computers promise to solve certain linear-equation problems exponentially faster than classical computers using an algorithm called HHL (named after its inventors Harrow, Hassidim, and Lloyd), but current implementations either work only on tiny problem sizes or give inaccurate answers when scaled up. SAPO extends the HHL algorithm by weaving in standard financial mathematics (mean-variance theory, which formalizes the risk-return trade-off) directly into the quantum circuit design so that the equations the quantum computer solves are already in a form that maps efficiently to the available quantum hardware. It also estimates the smallest and largest meaningful eigenvalues (a measure of the problem's numerical scale) from historical market data and uses those estimates to tune the circuit parameters, sharpening accuracy. The goal is to make quantum linear solvers practical for realistic financial problem sizes.
